items.stimulus: The Gauge at Pell Point is an 1894 novel by Harriet Coyle. Its main character, Nell Ambry, lives in a lighthouse on a rocky coast and keeps the daily weather log that her father began decades earlier. The log records rainfall, wind direction and air pressure for passing ships. Most of the novel takes place over one harsh winter. In an essay on the book, a literary critic claims that Nell keeps her weather records faithfully even when the conditions make the work unpleasant.
items.stem: Which quotation from The Gauge at Pell Point most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Nell loved the quiet hour after a storm, when the clouds broke apart and the harbor lay still and silver beneath them."
"Her father had kept the logbook for thirty years, and its pages had gone brown and soft from the damp of the tower."
"Though the sleet stung her cheeks and numbed her fingers, Nell climbed to the gauge at dawn and wrote down every figure."
"On mild mornings Nell would linger beside the barometer, idly tapping its glass and humming quietly to herself."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Nell keeps her records faithfully, and she does so even when conditions are unpleasant. In this line the sleet stings and numbs her (unpleasant conditions), yet she climbs to the gauge and records every figure (faithful record-keeping). It is the only choice that shows both parts.

D.why: Nell is near the instruments here, but the mornings are mild and she is idling, not recording. This shows only half the claim at most and leaves out the unpleasant conditions entirely.

items.stimulus: The Valley Songbook is a 1931 novel by Tomas Varga. It follows Anselm Reiter, a musicologist who spends years collecting folk ballads from mountain villages before they are forgotten. Other scholars in the novel compete to publish first and to have collections named after themselves. Reiter is different. According to one reviewer, Reiter cares more about keeping the songs alive than about receiving credit for collecting them.
items.stem: Which quotation from The Valley Songbook most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: Reiter spent whole winters traveling from village to village, his notebook tucked inside his coat against the cold.
"I do not mind if no one recalls who wrote these tunes down," Reiter said, "so long as someone is still singing them."
Reiter was delighted when the city paper printed his portrait above a long article praising his new collection.
The oldest singer in the valley knew forty ballads, each of which she had learned as a girl from her own grandmother.

items.stimulus: On the Training of Runners is a 1908 book by the track coach Walter Prentiss. At the time, many coaches assumed that athletes improved simply by running as many miles as possible. items.stem: Which quotation from On the Training of Runners most effectively illustrates the claim?

"No athlete ever won a race by training only when the mood suited him; the work must be done daily, in all weather."
"Sleep is a pleasant indulgence for the idle, but it does nothing to build the strength that a racer truly needs."
"The hard mile and the long sleep are partners in the making of a runner; neglect either one, and he will not improve."

items.stimulus: "The Surveyor's Confession" is an 1887 poem by Edwin Marlowe. Its speaker is an aging mapmaker who has spent his life charting a small coastal town. Looking over his finished map, the speaker reflects on what his careful work achieved. items.stem: Which quotation from "The Surveyor's Confession" most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "My ink was black, my paper smooth and fine, / And I worked by candle long into the night."
"I drew each river's bend and every hill, / But not the voices calling down the lane."
"The finished chart held all the town contained— / Its songs, its fires, the faces at the door."
"Beyond the hills there lay a land unknown, / Whose roads no surveyor ever walked."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: the map is accurate, and it still fails to capture the town's life. In the first half of the line he drew every bend and hill (accuracy). C.why: This line says the map captured everything, including songs and faces. That reverses the claim that the map cannot capture the town's life.

D.why: This line is about unmapped land beyond the town. That is a different limitation, not the one in the claim, which is the map's failure to capture the town's own life.

per_choice.B: You have the repeated-test half: three loadings, the same result, and a number she accepts. No authority appears, so the line can't show her refusing to accept a published figure.
per_choice.D: Building by feel and memory goes against Voss's reliance on measurement. The line also comes from her father, not her, so it shows nothing about her habit of mind.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: In The Diet Kitchen (1923), dietitian Marguerite Lowell draws on two decades of running a children's convalescent home. The book was written partly to correct the nutrition pamphlets of the day, which relied on explaining to children why certain foods were healthful. Lowell holds that children come to eat a food by watching adults enjoy it, not by hearing that it is good for them: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The Diet Kitchen most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Tell a child that spinach builds the blood and he will believe every word of it, and leave it on his plate."
"A child will copy the adult who feeds him in nearly everything, from how he holds a fork to when he sleeps."
"Children who were allowed to choose their own vegetables at market ate more of them at supper that night."
"One boy ate turnips for a month because I ate them in front of him, plainly and with relish, and said nothing."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: (1) children take up a food by watching an adult enjoy it, and (2) not through being told it is healthful. In D, the boy eats turnips "because I ate them in front of him," which is the watching. "With relish" is the enjoyment, and "said nothing" rules out telling. All of it is shown in one line.

A.why: This line shows that telling fails, which is the second half of the claim, and its wry tone sounds like Lowell. It never shows what does work: no adult eats anything, and no child takes up a food. This is the half-the-claim trap.

B.why: This is imitation in general, applied to forks and bedtimes. The claim is narrower: watching an adult enjoy a particular food. A broad statement about copying doesn't show that narrower point, and it leaves out the contrast with telling.

C.why: This credits choosing for oneself, which is a different explanation for why children eat a food. No adult is shown eating anything, so the line doesn't support Lowell's claim.
